learningObjectives.title: Medieval and early modern public health
Modern public health and the welfare state

questions.q: In the Middle Ages, which theory blamed disease on 'bad air' or unpleasant smells?
questions.explain: Medieval people believed miasma, or bad air from rotting matter and filth, was a cause of disease.

questions.q: In which years did the Black Death first reach England?
questions.explain: The Black Death first struck England in 1348-49, killing roughly a third to a half of the population.

questions.q: Why did many medieval monasteries enjoy better public health than nearby towns?
options: They had clean water supplies, latrines and drainage systems
They had trained doctors who understood germs
They banned all sick people from entering
They were built on higher, colder ground
questions.explain: Wealthy, orderly monasteries piped in clean water and sited latrines away from drinking supplies.

questions.q: A 14th-century townsperson is fined for dumping household waste into the town ditch. This punishment reflects which measure?
questions.explain: The Statute of Cambridge (1388) was an early national attempt to stop waste being dumped in ditches and rivers.

questions.q: During the Great Plague of 1665, how were houses containing infected people marked?
options: With a red cross painted on the door
With a black flag on the roof
With a bell hung on the gate
questions.explain: Infected houses were shut up and marked with a red cross and the words 'Lord have mercy upon us'.

questions.q: Which response to the Great Plague of 1665 shows continuity with medieval ideas about disease?
options: Believing the plague was a punishment sent by God
Setting up a General Board of Health
questions.explain: Religious explanations persisted from the medieval period, showing continuity in beliefs about disease.

questions.q: A source describes 'searchers of the dead' examining bodies and recording deaths in weekly Bills of Mortality. Which event does this most likely relate to?
questions.explain: Bills of Mortality recorded plague deaths in London parishes during outbreaks such as that of 1665.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1842 Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population?
questions.explain: Chadwick's 1842 report argued that dirt and poor living conditions caused disease and drove the case for reform.

questions.q: Why is the 1848 Public Health Act often described as limited or weak?
options: It was permissive, so towns did not have to set up boards of health
It banned the building of any new sewers
It only applied to the city of London
questions.explain: Because the Act was voluntary rather than compulsory, many towns simply ignored it.

questions.q: A doctor plots cholera deaths on a street map, notices they cluster around one water pump, and has its handle removed. Who was this?
questions.explain: In 1854 John Snow linked a Soho cholera outbreak to the Broad Street pump and removed its handle.

questions.q: What did John Snow's Broad Street investigation help to prove?
options: That cholera was spread through contaminated water, not bad air
That cholera was caused by miasma
That cholera was a punishment from God
That cholera could be cured by bloodletting
questions.explain: Snow's evidence pointed to dirty water as the means of transmission, challenging miasma theory.

questions.q: The Great Stink of 1858 prompted the building of London's new sewer network, engineered by whom?
questions.explain: Bazalgette designed London's system of sewers and embankments to carry waste away from the city.

questions.q: How did the 1875 Public Health Act differ from the 1848 Act?
options: It was compulsory, forcing local authorities to improve sanitation
It abolished all local boards of health
It applied only to rural areas
It made health care free for everyone
questions.explain: The 1875 Act made duties such as providing clean water and sewers compulsory for local authorities.

questions.q: Why was Louis Pasteur's Germ Theory (1861) important for public health?
options: It gave a scientific reason to clean up dirt and prevent disease
It proved that miasma caused all diseases
It ended the need for sewers
It introduced the theory of the four humours
questions.explain: Germ Theory showed that microbes caused disease, strengthening the case for sanitary reform.

questions.q: In 1876 a town council is legally required to appoint a Medical Officer of Health and provide clean water and drainage. Which law made these duties compulsory?
questions.explain: The 1875 Public Health Act compelled local authorities to appoint officials and provide sanitation.

questions.q: Why was Seebohm Rowntree's 1901 study of poverty in York significant?
options: It showed poverty was often caused by low wages and illness, not laziness
It proved poverty did not exist in Britain
It blamed the poor for their own suffering
questions.explain: Rowntree's evidence challenged the idea that poverty was simply the fault of the poor and encouraged reform.

questions.q: Why did the Boer War (1899-1902) increase concern about public health?
options: Many army recruits were found to be unfit for service
It caused a cholera epidemic in London
It made food shortages worse at home
questions.explain: The poor physical condition of many recruits raised fears about national health and efficiency.

questions.q: The Liberal government's Old Age Pensions Act was passed in which year?
questions.explain: The 1908 Old Age Pensions Act gave a small weekly pension to poorer people over 70.

questions.q: Which of these was one of the 'five giants' identified in the 1942 Beveridge Report?
questions.explain: Beveridge's five giants were Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness.

questions.q: Who was the Minister of Health who oversaw the creation of the NHS in 1948?
questions.explain: Aneurin (Nye) Bevan led the launch of the National Health Service, free at the point of use, in 1948.
